name: Humanin

lead: Humanin is a small peptide made from mitochondrial DNA, discovered in 2001 during Alzheimer research.
Lab and animal work links it to cell survival and insulin action. No human trials have tested it as a treatment or for looks or longevity.

paras: It is reported to block apoptosis by interfering with Bax [3] and to act on cell-surface receptors including formyl peptide receptors [4].
No human safety data from treatment trials were found; some research reports it may impair chemotherapy and promote tumor growth in cancer models [1]. It is not an approved drug.

lead: Humanin is a short peptide encoded within mitochondrial DNA, in the gene for 16S ribosomal RNA, and was the first mitochondria-derived peptide identified [1][2]. It was discovered in 2001 by several groups studying different questions, including protection of neurons against Alzheimer-related toxicity [3], interaction with the apoptosis protein Bax [4] and with IGFBP-3 [5].

Laboratory and animal research has linked it to cell protection, insulin sensitivity and inflammation [6][7][8]. It is not an approved drug; the studies found are cell, animal and observational human work, and no trials were found of humanin as a treatment or for appearance.

paras: A 2001 expression screen identified a gene whose product protected neuronal cells from death caused by familial Alzheimer disease genes and amyloid-beta [3][9]. In 2003 humanin was reported to suppress apoptosis by interfering with Bax activation [4] and to bind IGFBP-3 [5]. It is also a ligand for the formyl peptide receptor family [10].

Reviews describe humanin as a mitochondrial signaling peptide, with a later-found counterpart, MOTS-c, also encoded in mitochondrial DNA [7][2][8]. Work in rodents reported a central role in regulating peripheral insulin action [2], and a 2016 study reported that mitochondrial-derived peptide levels vary with age and relate to apoptosis, insulin sensitivity and inflammatory markers [6]. A transcriptome study of major depression and suicide is also listed among humanin-related literature [11]. Some research cited on Wikipedia reports that humanin may impair chemotherapy and promote tumor growth in certain cancers [1].

No studies found of humanin administered as a treatment. Registered human studies are observational, measuring humanin levels in acute kidney injury, cardiac surgery and renal transplantation [12][13][14]. Evidence for any appearance or longevity effect in people is not available.

timeline.event: Humanin reported as a neuroprotective rescue factor [3].
Bax interaction and IGFBP-3 binding reported [4][5].
MOTS-c described, extending the mitochondrial-peptide concept [7].
